subtopic_detail: Cyclical lower abdominal pain with absent menarche and normal secondary sexual development
stem:
You are the paediatric and adolescent gynaecology registrar seeing a 14 year old girl brought by her mother because she has never had a period and has had monthly lower abdominal pain for six months.

The pain lasts three to four days each month and is now severe enough that she has missed school on several occasions. Her mother says her daughter has recently started complaining of difficulty passing urine on the worst days. Breast development began at eleven and both breast and pubic hair development are at the adult stage. She is on the 60th centile for height, has no headaches or visual symptoms, and has a normal sense of smell. Abdominal examination reveals a smooth suprapubic mass rising to just below the umbilicus, and she is not sexually active.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 5 breast and pubic hair development, height on the 60th centile, smooth non tender suprapubic mass palpable to just below the umbilicus, external genitalia otherwise not yet inspected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Inspect the external genitalia with the parent present and arrange pelvic ultrasound the same day
options.rationale: Cyclical pain with primary amenorrhoea, normal secondary sexual characteristics and a suprapubic mass indicates outflow obstruction with accumulating menstrual blood, and inspection of the introitus will show a bulging bluish membrane if the obstruction is at the hymen. Ultrasound confirms the level of obstruction and the presence of a normal uterus and ovaries, which together determine whether a simple incision or complex reconstruction is needed. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Measure follicle stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone and oestradiol before performing any examination
options.rationale: Gonadotrophin measurement is the correct pathway when secondary sexual characteristics are absent or incomplete, because it separates gonadal failure from hypothalamic causes. Fully developed secondary characteristics with cyclical pain indicate a functioning axis and shift the question to outflow. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Request a karyotype and serum testosterone to investigate a disorder of sexual development in this girl
options.rationale: Karyotype and androgen measurement are directed at complete androgen insensitivity, in which pubic hair is characteristically sparse or absent and there is no uterus, so no menstrual blood accumulates and cyclical pain does not occur. Adult pubic hair with cyclical pain argues against it. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress the cycle and relieve the monthly pain she describes
options.rationale: Cycle suppression would reduce further accumulation but leaves an obstructed collection and its complications untreated, including retrograde flow and urinary retention. Hormonal suppression is a holding measure only after the anatomy is known. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis as the initial imaging test to define the anatomy
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable for complex obstructive anomalies and for planning reconstruction, but ultrasound is the appropriate first test and is quicker and more accessible. Imaging by magnetic resonance is added when ultrasound shows a complex or higher level obstruction. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea is approached first by asking whether secondary sexual characteristics are present, because that single question splits the differential. Absent or incomplete development points towards gonadal failure or hypothalamic pituitary causes and is investigated with gonadotrophins, oestradiol and karyotype. Normal development with cyclical pain points instead to an obstructed outflow tract, in which menstrual blood accumulates and produces a suprapubic mass, and pressure effects such as urinary retention or constipation. Imperforate hymen is the commonest such obstruction and is recognised at inspection as a tense bluish bulging membrane, while transverse vaginal septum and cervical agenesis sit higher and need magnetic resonance imaging and specialist reconstruction. Definitive treatment of an imperforate hymen is surgical incision with drainage, performed by a gynaecologist rather than at the bedside, after which menstruation and fertility are typically normal.
key_points: Presence of secondary sexual characteristics divides the differential in primary amenorrhoea
Cyclical pain with a suprapubic mass indicates accumulating obstructed menstrual blood
Urinary retention and constipation are pressure complications of a large collection
Inspection of the introitus is the diagnostic step for imperforate hymen
Higher obstructions such as transverse septum need magnetic resonance imaging and reconstruction
explanation.pearls: Never incise or aspirate a bulging obstructing membrane at the bedside or in the emergency department, because inadequate drainage through a small opening allows ascending infection of a large blood collection under pressure, and definitive hymenotomy with full drainage in theatre is the operation that preserves subsequent reproductive function.

subtopic_detail: Vaginal bulge in an older woman with significant comorbidity declining an operation
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 78 year old woman who describes a dragging sensation and a lump she can feel at the vaginal entrance by the end of each day. It has been present for a year and now interferes with her gardening.

She has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease requiring home oxygen at night, and her cardiologist has documented an ejection fraction of 35 percent. She has been told she is a poor anaesthetic candidate and says clearly that she does not want an operation. On examination there is descent of the anterior vaginal wall to 1 cm beyond the hymen on straining, with a well oestrogenised appearance following six weeks of topical oestrogen prescribed by her general practitioner. She empties her bladder completely and has no incontinence, no bleeding and no ulceration of the vaginal skin.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, BP 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Anterior vaginal wall descent to 1 cm beyond the hymen on Valsalva, vaginal epithelium well oestrogenised, no ulceration, post void residual volume 30 mL
data_table.Investigations: Post void residual 30 mL on bladder scan, urinalysis negative for nitrites and leucocytes

options.text: Referral for colpocleisis as an obliterative procedure carrying lower operative risk than reconstruction
options.rationale: Colpocleisis is a legitimate option for frail women who no longer wish to be sexually active and does carry lower risk than reconstruction, yet it remains an operation that she has declined. It becomes relevant only if conservative management fails and she reconsiders surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

options.text: Fitting of a vaginal support pessary with a planned review to check fit and vaginal skin condition
options.rationale: A pessary is the appropriate first line for symptomatic prolapse in a woman who declines surgery or is a poor operative candidate, and it can relieve the bulge symptom immediately without anaesthetic risk. Her vaginal epithelium is already well oestrogenised, which improves tolerance, and scheduled review detects erosion early. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

options.text: Referral for anterior colporrhaphy under regional anaesthesia to minimise the perioperative risk involved
options.rationale: Regional technique reduces but does not remove the risk in a woman with severe airways disease and impaired ventricular function, and she has clearly declined an operation. Her stated preference is a decisive part of the decision rather than an obstacle to work around. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

options.text: A supervised pelvic floor muscle training programme alone as definitive management of the bulge symptom
options.rationale: Pelvic floor training helps mild prolapse and is a valuable adjunct, but descent beyond the hymen is unlikely to be reversed by muscle training alone. It is offered alongside a pessary rather than instead of one at this stage. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

options.text: Continuation of topical vaginal oestrogen alone with review of her symptoms again in six months time
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen improves epithelial quality and comfort and supports pessary use but does not provide mechanical support for a descended wall. Six months of an ineffective single measure leaves her symptomatic and limits her activity further. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

explanation.summary: Management of pelvic organ prolapse is driven by symptoms rather than by the stage seen on examination, and the three broad options are observation, conservative treatment with pessary and pelvic floor training, and surgery. A pessary is first line for any woman who declines surgery, is awaiting it, is a poor operative candidate or is pregnant or planning further pregnancy, and it can relieve the bulge sensation immediately. Ring pessaries are usually tried first for anterior and apical descent, with Gellhorn or other space filling types used when a ring will not retain. Topical vaginal oestrogen improves epithelial quality and reduces erosion, and regular review is essential because a neglected pessary can ulcerate or become embedded. Pelvic floor muscle training is a useful adjunct and is most effective for milder degrees of descent.
key_points: Prolapse is treated for symptoms, not for the stage recorded on examination
Pessary is first line for women declining surgery or unfit for anaesthesia
Topical vaginal oestrogen improves epithelial quality and pessary tolerance
Scheduled review is mandatory to detect erosion or an embedded device
Pelvic floor training is an adjunct and works best for mild descent
explanation.pearls: Book the first pessary review within two to four weeks and then at least six monthly, because an unreviewed device can erode into the bladder or rectum and produce a fistula, and a woman who moves into residential care or develops cognitive impairment is the classic patient in whom a forgotten pessary is found years later.

subtopic_detail: Rapidly progressive coarse hair growth with clitoral change in a woman in her thirties
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34 year old woman with coarse dark hair on her chin, upper lip and lower abdomen. She says the change began about eight months ago and has accelerated, and that she now shaves daily when previously she needed nothing.

Her periods were regular every 28 days until six months ago and she has had none for the past three months. She has noticed her voice sounding deeper on recordings and that her hairline has receded at the temples. She takes no medications, no supplements and no androgenic preparations, and there is no family history of excess hair growth. Her body mass index is 23 kg per square metre and there are no violaceous striae, no proximal weakness and no facial rounding. On examination the clitoris measures 9 mm in transverse diameter.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Coarse terminal hair on chin, upper lip and lower abdomen, temporal hairline recession, clitoral transverse diameter 9 mm, body mass index 23 kg per square metre, no striae or proximal myopathy
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), prolactin 340 mIU/L (less than 500)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for laser hair reduction and reassure her that this pattern is a common familial variation
options.rationale: Idiopathic and familial hirsutism develops gradually, does not cause voice change or clitoromegaly, and is not accompanied by new amenorrhoea. Cosmetic treatment without investigation would leave a potentially serious cause unexamined. (Source: RANZCOG: Hirsutism and virilisation)

options.text: Measure early morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone alone to investigate for non classical adrenal hyperplasia
options.rationale: This measurement is a sensible part of the workup of hirsutism with menstrual disturbance, and non classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia is a genuine cause. It does not on its own address a virilising picture, in which the priority is to identify or exclude a tumour. (Source: RANZCOG: Hirsutism and virilisation)

options.text: Measure total testosterone with dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate and arrange pelvic and adrenal imaging
options.rationale: Rapid onset hirsutism over months with voice deepening, temporal recession and clitoromegaly is virilisation, which signals a marked androgen excess and raises the possibility of an androgen secreting ovarian or adrenal tumour. Measuring testosterone alongside the adrenal androgen indicates the likely source, and imaging of both ovaries and adrenals follows without delay. (Source: RANZCOG: Hirsutism and virilisation)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill with an antiandrogenic progestogen and review after six months
options.rationale: This is appropriate treatment for the gradual hirsutism of polycystic ovary syndrome, which develops slowly from adolescence without virilising features. Suppressing symptoms in a woman with rapidly progressive virilisation risks masking a tumour for six months. (Source: RANZCOG: Hirsutism and virilisation)

options.text: Arrange an overnight dexamethasone suppression test as the first investigation of the androgen excess
options.rationale: Cortisol excess is suggested by violaceous striae, proximal myopathy, facial rounding and easy bruising, and none of these are present in a woman with a normal body mass index. It is a reasonable later test but not the first line of enquiry for virilisation. (Source: RANZCOG: Hirsutism and virilisation)

explanation.summary: Hirsutism describes excess terminal hair in an androgen dependent distribution, and the overwhelming majority of cases are polycystic ovary syndrome or idiopathic, both of which evolve slowly from around puberty. Virilisation is a different clinical category and is defined by deepening of the voice, temporal balding, clitoromegaly, increased muscle bulk and breast atrophy, which together indicate a much higher circulating androgen concentration. Rapid onset over months with virilising features shifts the concern towards an androgen secreting ovarian or adrenal tumour, and to ovarian hyperthecosis in postmenopausal women. Investigation is with total testosterone and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate to indicate the source, with early imaging of the ovaries by transvaginal ultrasound and of the adrenals by computed tomography. Cosmetic and hormonal suppressive treatments are correct for the common causes but must not be started before a virilising presentation has been investigated.
key_points: Slow hirsutism from puberty suggests polycystic ovary syndrome or an idiopathic cause
Voice change, temporal recession and clitoromegaly define virilisation
Rapid onset over months raises concern for an androgen secreting tumour
Testosterone with dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate indicates ovarian versus adrenal source
Image ovaries and adrenals early rather than starting suppressive treatment
explanation.pearls: A markedly raised dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate points towards an adrenal source while a very high testosterone with a normal adrenal androgen points towards the ovary, and a normal transvaginal ultrasound does not exclude a small androgen secreting ovarian tumour, so persistent virilisation with high testosterone warrants specialist review and consideration of selective venous sampling.

subtopic_detail: Three first trimester losses with a uterine cavity abnormality seen on two dimensional imaging
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 31 year old woman referred after three consecutive first trimester miscarriages, each at around nine weeks with foetal heart activity previously seen.

Her partner is the same for all three pregnancies and she has no living children. Her cycles are regular, she has never had pelvic infection or uterine instrumentation apart from one suction curettage, and her body mass index is 24 kg per square metre. Two dimensional transvaginal ultrasound reports a possible partition within the uterine cavity, and the sonographer notes that the external uterine contour could not be clearly assessed on that view. Antiphospholipid antibodies measured twelve weeks apart are negative, both parental karyotypes are normal, and her thyroid function and glycated haemoglobin are within the reference range.

data_table.Examination: Normal vulva, vagina and cervix, uterus anteverted and normal in size, no adnexal masses, no pelvic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Lupus anticoagulant negative, anticardiolipin and anti beta 2 glycoprotein antibodies negative on two occasions twelve weeks apart, parental karyotypes normal, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), glycated haemoglobin 5.1 percent (less than 6.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Hysterosalpingography to outline the uterine cavity and to confirm that both fallopian tubes are patent
options.rationale: This outlines the cavity and shows tubal patency but is equally unable to demonstrate the external fundal contour, producing the same ambiguity. Tubal patency is also not the question in a woman who conceives readily. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Endometrial biopsy with culture to investigate chronic endometritis as a contributor to the losses
options.rationale: Chronic endometritis is an area of active research in recurrent loss but testing and treating it is not established practice, and it does not explain a structural finding already visible on imaging. The abnormality identified should be characterised first. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Products of conception karyotyping arranged prospectively should a further pregnancy loss occur
options.rationale: Cytogenetic testing of pregnancy tissue is informative and is offered in recurrent loss, but it requires another miscarriage to happen and answers a different question from the one raised by an abnormal cavity. It complements rather than replaces defining the anomaly now. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Three dimensional transvaginal ultrasound to define the cavity outline together with the fundal contour
options.rationale: Distinguishing a septum from a bicornuate uterus depends on the external fundal contour, which two dimensional imaging cannot reliably show, and three dimensional coronal reconstruction visualises the cavity and the serosal outline in a single non invasive test. The distinction is decisive because a septum is treated hysteroscopically while a bicornuate uterus is not. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Diagnostic hysteroscopy under general anaesthesia to inspect and record the appearance of the cavity
options.rationale: Hysteroscopy shows two horns from the inside whether the cause is a septum or a bicornuate uterus, so it cannot make the distinction alone and would need laparoscopy alongside it. It becomes the operative step once imaging has established that a septum is present. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

explanation.summary: A septate uterus is the congenital anomaly most consistently associated with recurrent first trimester loss, because implantation on the poorly vascularised fibrous septum leads to failure once the pregnancy demands greater perfusion. The essential distinction is from a bicornuate uterus, and it rests entirely on the external fundal contour, which is smooth or minimally indented in a septum and deeply cleft in a bicornuate uterus, while the internal view is identical. Two dimensional ultrasound and hysterosalpingography both image only the cavity and therefore cannot separate the two, whereas three dimensional coronal reconstruction shows cavity and serosal outline together and has become the investigation of choice. The distinction matters clinically because hysteroscopic septum resection is a straightforward day procedure associated with improved live birth rates in observational series, whereas a bicornuate uterus is not amenable to that operation. Renal tract anomalies coexist with Mullerian anomalies often enough that renal imaging is arranged when one is confirmed.
key_points: External fundal contour is the only feature separating septate from bicornuate uterus
Two dimensional ultrasound and hysterosalpingography image the cavity alone
Three dimensional coronal reconstruction shows cavity and serosal outline together
Hysteroscopic resection applies to a septum but not to a bicornuate uterus
Arrange renal tract imaging once a Mullerian anomaly is confirmed
explanation.pearls: Arrange renal tract ultrasound whenever a Mullerian anomaly is confirmed, because the paramesonephric and mesonephric systems develop together and unilateral renal agenesis accompanies a meaningful proportion of uterine anomalies, most classically in the obstructed hemivagina with ipsilateral renal agenesis syndrome.

subtopic_detail: Bone protection choice in a woman with ovarian failure well before the usual age
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 34 year old woman who stopped menstruating eighteen months ago and has had hot flushes and vaginal dryness since. Follicle stimulating hormone measured twice more than four weeks apart was elevated on both occasions with a low oestradiol.

Her bone density scan shows a lumbar spine Z score of minus 2.3. She has never had a fragility fracture, does not smoke, drinks minimal alcohol and walks daily. She has completed her family and uses condoms. She has no personal or family history of breast cancer, no history of venous thrombosis, and her blood pressure and lipids are normal. She has read online that hormone therapy causes breast cancer and asks whether she should take a bone medication instead.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70/min, BP 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 62 IU/L then 58 IU/L more than four weeks apart (follicular phase 3-10), oestradiol 42 pmol/L (follicular phase 90-400), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 74 nmol/L (greater than 50), lumbar spine Z score minus 2.3

lead_in: What would you first recommend for her bone health?

options.text: Weekly oral alendronate with calcium and vitamin D supplementation and repeat densitometry in two years
options.rationale: Bisphosphonates have a long skeletal half life and are avoided in young women of potentially reproductive age given uncertainty about foetal effects in a later pregnancy. They also leave the vasomotor symptoms, urogenital atrophy and cardiovascular consequences of oestrogen deficiency untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Six monthly subcutaneous denosumab with calcium and vitamin D and monitoring of bone turnover markers
options.rationale: Denosumab requires uninterrupted continuation because stopping it produces rapid bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures, a poor commitment for a woman of 34 with decades ahead. It is also directed at the bone alone and does not address the underlying hormone deficiency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Calcium and vitamin D supplementation with a resistance exercise programme and repeat scanning in five years
options.rationale: Nutritional and exercise measures are worthwhile adjuncts but cannot compensate for absent oestrogen, and her vitamin D and calcium are already adequate. Deferring definitive treatment for five years allows further bone loss during the years of peak consolidation. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously to suppress symptoms and to maintain bone density
options.rationale: Combined contraception is an acceptable alternative when a woman prefers it or needs contraception, but the ethinyloestradiol dose is supraphysiological and it appears less favourable than replacement therapy for bone density and blood pressure. It is second choice rather than first recommendation here. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature ovarian insufficiency)

options.text: Systemic oestrogen with a progestogen for endometrial protection, continued until the average age of menopause
options.rationale: Ovarian insufficiency before forty is treated with physiological hormone replacement continued at least until the average age of natural menopause, because these women are oestrogen deficient for decades and face excess fracture and cardiovascular risk without it. In this age group the therapy replaces what her ovaries should be producing and the breast cancer risk seen in older postmenopausal users does not transfer to her situation. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature ovarian insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Premature ovarian insufficiency is diagnosed before the age of forty on the basis of amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea with elevated follicle stimulating hormone on two occasions at least four weeks apart. It differs fundamentally from menopause at the usual age because these women face several additional decades of oestrogen deficiency, with consequences for bone density, cardiovascular risk, urogenital health, sexual function and possibly cognition. Hormone therapy is therefore replacement of a physiological deficiency rather than treatment of an age related change, and it is recommended until at least the average age of natural menopause unless contraindicated. The breast cancer signal observed in older postmenopausal users does not apply to replacement in this age group, and this reassurance is central to the consultation. Bone specific agents such as bisphosphonates and denosumab are reserved for women who cannot take oestrogen, with bisphosphonate use in young women complicated by the long skeletal half life.
key_points: Diagnosis needs elevated follicle stimulating hormone twice, at least four weeks apart, under forty
Hormone therapy here replaces a deficiency and continues to the average age of menopause
The breast cancer risk of later postmenopausal therapy does not transfer to this group
Bisphosphonates are avoided in young women because of the long skeletal half life
Use the Z score rather than the T score to interpret density in women under fifty
explanation.pearls: Counsel explicitly that hormone therapy is not contraception, because spontaneous ovarian activity returns intermittently in around five to ten percent of women with premature ovarian insufficiency and pregnancies do occur, so a woman who wishes to avoid conception needs a separate reliable method alongside her replacement therapy.
